title: The Elephant Gambit: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d5 and the idea
outcomes: Says what Black gives (a pawn, for now) and gets (time, space and pressure on the e-file) in the Elephant Gambit
Explains why 4.Qe2 matters (the pawn on e4 is pinned to the king) and finds Black's defending moves
Avoids the typical mistakes: taking back on d5 too early and defending with a pawn move
Reads engine numbers and online counts as evidence of different kinds, with their sample sizes

steps.prompt: As White, what would you play here? As Black, what do you hope for if White takes the pawn?

steps.text: **The question of this lesson.** The Elephant Gambit offers a pawn on move two. What does Black give, what does Black get, and why does one White reply matter so much? Afterwards you can explain the opening to a friend, give the engine's honest verdict and avoid the traps on both sides. Marks: [V] checked here, [S] a source, [I] inference, [H] a guess to test.

steps.text: **What Black gives and gets.** [I] Black gives a pawn for now, and spends three of the first three moves on pawns while White has one piece out. Black gets time: the pawn on e4 hits the knight, controls d3 and f3 and cramps White's development. Whether that is worth a pawn depends on one reply, so we look at it next.

steps.caption: White to move after 3...e4. The knight on f3 is attacked. White can retreat the knight, move it forward, or find something cleverer. Ask which move defends the knight and attacks the pawn at the same time.

4.Qe2 is a legal move.

steps.caption: Position after 4.Qe2, Black to move. The pawn on e4 attacks the knight, yet Black cannot take it. Look at the e-file: queen, pawn, king. Which squares can the pawn actually go to?

claims.statement: The pawn on e4 can move only to e3.
The capture 4...exf3 is illegal.

steps.title: Is the pawn on e4 pinned?
steps.prompt: Predict for each position, then check. One difference matters.

steps.text: **The idea behind 4.Qe2.** [I] A pin means a piece cannot (or should not) move because a more valuable piece stands behind it. Here the queen pins the black pawn to the king, so the threat against the knight disappears and White's queen attacks the pawn. That is why this reply matters most. Black needs a move that adds a defender to e4. Which one?

steps.caption: A line you may have seen: 4...f6?. The auto-captions of one video we read name this move with an exclamation mark [S-video, unverified]. Captions are unreliable, and the engine disagrees: the pawn on e4 is left alone.

line.say: The pawn guards e5 and g5, but not e4.
The queen takes the pawn with check, and White is two pawns up.

claims.statement: After 4...f6 no black piece defends e4.
4...f6 scores at least 250 cp worse than the best move (depth 16).

steps.title: Which move defends the pawn on e4?
steps.prompt: Predict for each position, then check.

steps.text: **Do not take back on d5 too early.** Black can win the pawn back with the queen at once, but then the knight comes to c3 and attacks the queen. After 4...Qxd5 5.Nc3 the queen has to move, and wherever it goes only the queen defends e4 while the queen and the knight attack it. The videos repeat this rule too [S-video, unverified]; the engine confirms it on the board below.

steps.caption: The recapture that fails. After 5.Nc3 the queen is attacked. Count the attackers and defenders of e4 before you answer.

The knight attacks the queen and the pawn on e4 together.

Only one black piece (the queen) defends e4.

steps.text: **Plans for both sides.** [I] White: take the pawn back only when the queen cannot be hit with tempo, develop the queenside knight, castle, and use the extra pawn after the queens are traded. Black: develop with threats on the e-file, castle, and look for the exchange that regains d5 or e4. [H] The gambit works best against a White player who forgets the queen move.

One engine, one depth; single runs differ by a few tenths. [I] The gambit costs Black about a pawn that is hard to win back: a modest edge, not a win. [H] It may score better than its number suggests when White must find several only-moves.

steps.prompt: Online, 4.Qe2 scores about 50% for White overall, but the engine says White is ahead. Does that mean the engine is wrong, or can a number like this have another cause? Write one cause and one test.

steps.text: **Counts are results, not verdicts.** [V] The 4.Qe2 score is 50% over 2,310 games, but it varies with the rating band: 51% at 2100 and above (170 games) and 60% below 1300 (190 games). Players choose the move, opponents err, and time limits differ. [I] A count tells you what people did; the engine tells you what a deep search found. Neither tells you the whole story, and we label both.

steps.text: **Typical mistakes.** [I] For Black: taking back on d5 too early, defending e4 with a pawn move, and forgetting the pin on the e-file. For White: retreating the knight and letting the pawn on e4 live, or taking on e4 at once. Each was shown above with the engine's verdict.

steps.caption: A tempting mistake for White: taking the pawn at once. After 6.dxe4 Qxe4 the queens can come off and Black has regained the pawn; the engine (depth 16) rates this lower than 6.Nbd2.

Black takes back with the queen and offers a trade of queens.

In our online data White chose 3.exd5 in 9,659 games and 3.Nxe5 in 4,052 (White score 49% after 3.Nxe5). The engine (depth 16) rates this position as a modest edge for White.

steps.text: **Who plays it, and where it comes from.** [S-video] Witty_Alien teaches and plays the Elephant Gambit in videos from 2025 and 2026. The move line in those videos is reconstructed from auto-captions and was only partly reproducible here; the engine rejected one move (4...f6) that the captions name. [R] Who first played the Elephant Gambit is not checked here, and we do not credit anyone as its inventor.

steps.prompt: [H] Is a gambit that the engine rates a pawn worse for the side that plays it still a good choice for a club player? Agree, disagree, or say what would test it.

steps.text: **Recap: what to remember.** The gambit offers a pawn for time. The key White reply, 4.Qe2, pins the e4 pawn to the king. Black defends with a knight and takes back on d5 only when the knight cannot come to c3 with tempo. The engine rates the main lines near +1.0 for White: a modest edge, not a refutation. Online counts show what people did, not what is best.

steps.prompt: Teach-back: in a few sentences, explain the Elephant Gambit to a friend. Say what Black gives and gets, when the idea works (and the pin that makes 4.Qe2 so good) and when it fails, give one position you could set up on a board, and name one mistake. Self-check afterwards: did you say when it works and when it fails, give an example, name a mistake? The app grades nothing; compare with the recap.
